card.hook: Here's a stadium called 'the chocolate box' where one stand looks sliced off at the edge, and that's exactly what makes this corner fun. It's the odd, layered view, not the postcard one.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Brandsen y Del Valle Iberlucea, on the stadium's west side. The middle of the stadium is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so face that way and you'll see the curved stands and the flank of the ground.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the curved stands in from close up. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched shot, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a stand edge or a mural.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line a stand edge up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean, and keep a bit of street at the bottom for scale.
card.best_time: Go in daytime on a day with no match, when the streets are quieter and easier to stand in.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the corner of Brandsen and Garibaldi and step well back from the stadium wall, because the farther you stand, the more of the stadium fits behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the stadium over your shoulder, ideally before sunset.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed during the stadium visit, though personal still photos are fine. Keep valuables out of sight, use your phone discreetly, and stick to main streets like Brandsen or Del Valle Iberlucea.
card.challenge: Can you get the curve of the stands sweeping across the frame, with every vertical line dead straight?
card.good_to_know: The stadium opened on 25 May 1940, and the 'chocolate box' nickname stuck after a third tier was finished in 1953. A fourth tier arrived in 1996, bringing capacity to 57,500. Boca's earlier ground stood on this very corner from 1924.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Brandsen y Del Valle Iberlucea, on the stadium's west side. The middle of the stadium is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so face that way and you'll see the curved stands and the flank of the ground.

card.hook: Imagine an opera house that took about twenty years to build, now sitting across a square where everyone seems to be crossing at once. That's the Teatro Colón from Plaza Lavalle, and the whole front and dome fit in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza Lavalle, on the Libertad side, facing the theatre, which lies to the south-east from there. Don't stand too close, or you'll tilt the phone up and the walls will lean inwards. One guide treats the Avenida 9 de Julio side as the back and this side as the front, so check on the day.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the facade and dome across the square. Switch to 0.5x only if people or trees block the full width. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the busts and carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest, because the facade is evenly lit. Early morning is usually quieter on the square. After dark, try night mode and rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza Lavalle, in the square in front of the theatre, with the main entrance on the Libertad side behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and let the theatre sit over your shoulder. It's a likely spot rather than a confirmed one, so check it looks right on the day.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the square from the main entrance, while you stand in front of it, so the full front of the theatre fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine from the public square, and personal-use photos are generally permitted. During performances it's strictly prohibited, and tour photos are generally allowed without flash. For tours or shows inside, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the facade and find a sculpted bust, then see if you can get it sharp while a crowd drifts past below.
card.good_to_know: The Teatro Colón opened on 25 May 1908 with Verdi's Aida. The busts and bas-reliefs on the facade are by Luigi Trinchero. It became a National Historic Monument in 1989, closed for a long refurbishment from 2006, and reopened in May 2010.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza Lavalle, on the Libertad side, facing the theatre, which lies to the south-east from there. card.hook: You walk through a pair of tall Doric columns and the photo is basically done before you've lifted your phone. The gates and stonework frame the lanes of tombs for you, which is a rare bit of help from a cemetery.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the main entrance portico on the Junín side, then face along the tree-lined lanes towards the mausoleums. Let the ironwork and columns frame the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole portico with the lanes beyond. If you're so close to the columns that they won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for statues, carvings and rooftops, so you don't have to lean over anything.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up a column or the gate with a vertical line so the whole portico stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light gives the gate nice shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the Tomb of Liliana Crociati inside the cemetery. Stand at the mausoleum where her statue sits beside her dog, use the front camera, and keep the tomb's Gothic facade behind you over your shoulder. 0.5x on the front camera helps fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the path in front of the main entrance gate and ask someone to step back and shoot, so the gate's ironwork and entrance frame you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally allowed, but keep flash off and never point it at tombs or mausoleums. Don't touch, climb on or enter the tombs, even if a door looks open, and stay quiet and discreet around anyone visiting a grave. Carry water, especially in summer, and skip rainy days because there's little shelter. Access and entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Cat hunt: about a dozen stray cats live here (as of 2024), so see if you can spot one among the marble and snap it from a respectful distance.
card.good_to_know: Recoleta Cemetery opened in 1822 as the first public cemetery in Buenos Aires, in the old garden of a convent. The convent's church, Our Lady of the Pillar, dates from 1732. Today it covers about 5.5 hectares with 4691 vaults, all above ground, and 94 of them are National Historical Monuments.

card.hook: Yes, it really is pink, and it's the kind of pink that makes strangers stop mid-stride and reach for their phones. The square in front is wide and open, so you can step back and fit the whole long building in one shot.
card.stand_here: Head for the Plaza de Mayo; the Casa Rosada is about 3 minutes on foot and straight ahead. Stand in the central part of the square, facing east, with the Pirámide de Mayo in front of you and the pink facade across the open plaza.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole facade with the pyramid in front. If the building feels cut off at the sides, drop to 0.5x for more square and sky. Go to 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the balcony and the flags.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the pyramid low in the frame and let the facade run along the upper third, then tap the pink wall and slide a bit darker if the sky is bright so the pink stays soft.
card.best_time: Early morning is the usual advice, anywhere from just after sunrise to around 8-10am, so check the light on the day. On national holidays the building may be lit in different colours at night.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Pirámide de Mayo in the middle of the square, with the Casa Rosada facade behind the pyramid. Use the front camera, hold it low and tilt up, and try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the open middle of the Plaza de Mayo looking toward the palace, while you stand between them and the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Interior tours are no longer offered, so shoot from outside. A fence is sometimes put up across the plaza, so check when you arrive. The square is generally busy enough to feel safe, but the area is mainly a transit zone after dark.
card.challenge: Get the pyramid, the pink facade and zero strangers' heads in one frame. If a fence is in the way, walk along the plaza and look for a gap.
card.good_to_know: The Casa Rosada is the Argentine president's official workplace and a National Historic Monument. The pink was reportedly chosen under President Sarmiento. It reached its present form in 1898, when it was enlarged and joined to the neighbouring Central Post Office.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Plaza de Mayo; the Casa Rosada is about 3 minutes on foot and straight ahead. Stand in the central part of the square, facing east, with the Pirámide de Mayo in front of you and the pink facade across the open plaza.

card.hook: You'll spot it from blocks away: one clean white needle, wide avenues on every side, and a hedge at its feet that spells out 'BA'. It's the shape most people picture when they think of Buenos Aires.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la República, in front of the monument beside the green 'BA' letters. The Obelisco is to your south-west, so face that way and let it rise straight up behind the letters.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the tower and the 'BA' letters sit together naturally. Switch to 0.5x to make the letters big in the foreground and fit the whole height of the tower in. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tip against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the tower and slide a little darker so the pale concrete keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Dusk or early evening is the most atmospheric, when the Obelisco is lit and the signs are glowing. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in front of you.
card.selfie_here: Head to the green 'BA' hedge letters in the small park at the base of the Obelisco and stand between the 'B' and the 'A'. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you want to squeeze the whole tower in, and let it rise behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the corner of Avenida Corrientes and Carlos Pellegrini, a popular point for photographing the Obelisco, especially at night when the theatre lights are on, and check the map for your exact spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Shoot from the pavement, the crosswalks or the central islands, and never step into the avenue for a better angle. Avenida 9 de Julio has heavy traffic, so use the designated crosswalks. If you want the high view from the Hotel Marriott, check that public access is still allowed first.
card.challenge: Stand between the 'B' and the 'A' and get the whole needle in the shot, tip included, with no stranger's head poking in. Harder than it sounds!
card.good_to_know: The Obelisco was built in 1936 to mark 400 years since the city's first foundation. Architect Alberto Prebisch designed it, and the German-led building team finished the 67.5-metre concrete tower in just 31 days. The site was once a church dedicated to St Nicholas of Bari, where the Argentine flag was first raised in the city in 1812, and an inscription on the north side records it.

card.hook: Caminito is only about 150 m long, so the colours come at you all at once, and so do the tango performers who'll happily wander into your shot. You can see most of it in a few minutes, so make the first one count.

card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds arrive, and you've got the best shot at fewer people in the frame. Plan it for daylight.
card.selfie_here: Stand about 4-5 m in front of the alfajor shop on the Magallanes corner, so the painted street sits at an angle behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want more of the colourful lane over your shoulder.

card.hook: Most people shoot Plaza de Mayo from down in the crowd, but the best view is from up high. From there the whole square lines up like a stage set, with the pink Casa Rosada at the far end.
card.stand_here: Head to the Cabildo de Buenos Aires and go up to its upper-floor balcony or terrace, which overlooks the square. Face east across the whole plaza, straight at the Casa Rosada.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full, balanced view. Try zoom 2x to pick out the Casa Rosada and cut the empty foreground (higher zooms depend on your phone). Only use zoom 0.5x if nobody's leaning on the balcony rail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the Casa Rosada on the centre line, then tap it and slide a bit darker if the sky is bright so the pink keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Guides disagree: some like late afternoon, others early morning. Try late afternoon, when the sun is likely behind you and lighting up the facade, then come back in the morning if the crowds are thin.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Casa Rosada on the square's central axis, facing away from it, so the pink facade is behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the building over your shoulder. For a cleaner angle with fewer tourists, try the fountain at the northeastern corner of the plaza. These spots come from guides describing where to photograph the building, so check them when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the plaza's western edge beside the Pirámide de Mayo and shoot east, while you stand out in the square with the Casa Rosada behind you so the whole facade fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the public areas of the plaza, but restrictions may apply inside museums or government buildings, so check before shooting inside the Cabildo. Keep your bag in front of your body, especially where tour groups gather near the Cabildo and the Casa Rosada fence. The square is a protest site, so fences or banners can block some spots.
card.challenge: Take one shot from down in the square with the Pirámide de Mayo as your foreground, then see if you can beat it from the Cabildo balcony.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de Mayo is the main square of Buenos Aires, and the Casa Rosada is the seat of the President of Argentina. The square took its modern form in 1884, when a colonnade that split it in two was pulled down. The Pirámide de Mayo in the middle went up in 1811 and was the city's first national monument.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Cabildo de Buenos Aires and go up to its upper-floor balcony or terrace, which overlooks the square. Face east across the whole plaza, straight at the Casa Rosada.

card.hook: You walk in for a book and end up staring at a painted ceiling, with crimson stage curtains straight ahead and old theatre boxes full of people reading. Yes, it's still a bookshop, and yes, your phone is going to get a workout.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits at the bookshop itself, on Santa Fe Avenue in Barrio Norte, so head inside. Stand on the main floor near the middle of the room and face the stage and café to get the curtains and boxes.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full height of the room in one go. Switch to 1x for the shelves and boxes, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the ceiling painting and the carved figures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the columns and boxes standing straight, then tap the bright stage lights and drag a little darker so the curtains keep their red.
card.best_time: Try a weekday morning, when it's likely to be quieter. The light inside is mostly artificial, so the time of day matters less for the light than for the crowds.
card.selfie_here: Head to the upper balcony and stand a step left or right of the middle, since the crowd gathers dead centre. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the bookstore spread out behind you over your shoulder. The café on the old stage is a good second spot, with the hall opening out behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Skip the flash and don't block the aisles for your photo. Check the official site before you go for current opening arrangements and any rules about photography inside.
card.challenge: Find three different frames in this one room: one wide shot, one ceiling shot and one of a reader tucked into an old theatre box.
card.good_to_know: This building opened in May 1919 as the Teatro Gran Splendid. In 1929 it showed the first sound films presented in Argentina. The old auditorium floor now holds bookshelves, and National Geographic named it the world's most beautiful bookstore in 2019.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits at the bookshop itself, on Santa Fe Avenue in Barrio Norte, so head inside. Stand on the main floor near the middle of the room and face the stage and café to get the curtains and boxes.

card.hook: Picture a hand-painted sign above a stall, with shoppers drifting past underneath. That's the Mercado de San Telmo, and you can get a dozen different photos here in a few minutes just by walking.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits at the market itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Start at an entrance or a wide spot in an aisle and face down the length of the market.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for most stall and aisle shots. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the full width of an aisle, and zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details across a counter without leaning into anyone's space.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines in your camera app and line them up with the aisle so the verticals stay straight and the rows of stalls lead the eye.
card.best_time: Go when the market is open but not too packed, so you can move freely. Daytime gives you the best natural light, and it's worth checking opening times locally before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little higher than usual. Let a colourful stall or sign sit over your shoulder, then check that your face isn't in shadow before you shoot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the corner of Bolívar and Carlos Calvo streets, where the market's entrances are in view, while you stand in front of the entrances.
card.rules_and_safety: On Sundays the feria is crowded and pickpockets are a real risk, so stay alert and keep your phone close. Ask before you take a portrait of a stallholder (a smile helps), and check locally for opening times and entry rules.
card.challenge: Find a hand-painted sign, then frame it so the aisle leads your eye straight to it, with one person walking away in the background.
card.good_to_know: The Mercado de San Telmo is a market in the San Telmo district of Buenos Aires. Its charm is the stalls, produce and goods, shop signs and visitors browsing the aisles. Wipe your phone's camera before you start, because market interiors can be dusty or greasy.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits at the market itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Start at an entrance or a wide spot in an aisle and face down the length of the market.

card.hook: Here's a café where the building is the main attraction and the coffee comes second. Come for the dark wood and the old-fashioned fittings, and you'll leave with a camera roll full of them.
card.stand_here: Stand outside Café Tortoni at Avenida de Mayo 825, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Step back a little along the pavement and face the entrance so the doorway and the whole front fill your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x outside to fit the whole street front in. Inside, switch to 1x for tables and woodwork, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for details on the walls and ceiling.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and line the doorway up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight shows off the facade best. Inside, any time the café is open works, but it's easier to take photos when it's less busy.
card.selfie_here: Out front, stand on the pavement of Avenida de Mayo with the facade behind you, using the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone offers it). Inside, head downstairs to the Alfonsina Storni salon and squeeze in beside the life-size figures of Borges, Gardel and Storni.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement facing the café entrance, and you stand in front of the door so the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine inside, but be kind to other guests and staff, and skip intrusive shots. Photos may be restricted during the tango show, so check with staff. It's a working café, so access is for customers and may be limited at busy times. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get one photo where the doorway is perfectly straight against your gridlines, then one inside where the dark wood looks as rich as a chocolate bar.
card.good_to_know: The café first opened in 1858 and is named after a Parisian café on Boulevard des Italiens. It moved to this site in 1880, and the street front was redesigned in 1898 by Alejandro Christophersen. Today the basement is a stage for jazz and tango artists.

card.hook: Hell on the ground floor, heaven up top, and a lighthouse on the roof: this office tower was planned like a poem. Even if you never read Dante, it's easy to spot, because it rises well above its lower 1920s neighbours on the avenue.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement directly across the street from the facade, at the building's address (Avenida de Mayo 1370), and face south. From there the whole tower and facade fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole tower fits from across the avenue. Switch to 1x for a tighter shot of the facade, and if your phone has 2x-5x, use it to pick out the lighthouse and spire at the top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a bright daytime hour for the street shot. If you take a tour up top, the hour before sunset is the recommended time for the rooftop views.
card.selfie_here: We don't have a named selfie spot for this one. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt the phone up a little so the tower rises behind your shoulder. Take a few, because people and traffic keep wandering through.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take the whole facade from the corner of Avenida de Mayo and San José, a block from the palace, with you in the shot if the view is clear.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and watch for passers-by and traffic. The lighthouse and rooftop are only open on scheduled guided tours, which involve a lot of walking and stairs, so wear comfortable shoes and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a little space above the spire and the lower neighbours as a base, so the tower looks like it's winning a height contest.
card.good_to_know: Palacio Barolo was finished in 1923 and designed by Italian architect Mario Palanti for businessman Luis Barolo. It was the tallest building in South America when it opened, at 100 metres and 22 floors. The design follows Dante's Divine Comedy, with hell in the lower floors, purgatory in the middle and heaven at the top, under a lighthouse and a Southern Cross spire.

card.hook: Picture a white mast leaning back like it's mid-dip, with cables flowing off it. Calatrava said the bridge is a couple dancing the tango, and once he's told you, you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Puente de la Mujer itself, at the middle of the span, right where the phone icon sits. Face along the walkway so the curve leads your eye to the mast, then turn round for a shot looking back towards the city.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole white arch and the dockside towers into one frame. Switch to 1x for a natural view along the walkway. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the mast and cables.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the mast up with a vertical line so the tango dancer doesn't look like it's falling over.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or twilight, or stay on after dark when the bridge is lit. At sunset, tap the bridge and slide the brightness down a touch so the white keeps its detail and the sky stays rich.
card.selfie_here: Stand at either end of the bridge deck with the bridge behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your arm out a little so the arch fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: If you'd like the bridge next to the old Fragata Sarmiento ship, ask a passer-by on the side pier at Dock 3, near the ship, to take the shot while you pose on the bridge.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public footbridge, so give people crossing plenty of room. Check the official site before you go for closures and for times when the span is due to rotate.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once with walkers and once without, then pick the winner. Bonus points if the tilted mast looks like it's dancing.
card.good_to_know: The bridge crosses Dock 3 in Puerto Madero. Its central span can swing round by 90 degrees to let boats through. Building began in 1998, it opened on 20 December 2001, and it was declared a Cultural Heritage of the City of Buenos Aires in 2018.

card.hook: Picture a 23 m steel flower standing alone in a pond, with a second flower hanging upside down in the water below it. That reflection is why everyone's photos of this place look so good.
card.stand_here: Head into Plaza de las Naciones Unidas and stand on the northwest side, near the Law School colonnade. Face south, so the flower is in front of you and the Law School facade and columns are layered behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the flower with the colonnade behind it. Switch to 0.5x if you want the whole pool and all the petals in one frame, or try 2x to pull the facade in closer behind the flower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the petals, then drag the brightness slider down a little (darker) so the shiny steel doesn't glare.
card.best_time: The petals normally open at 8 in the morning and close at sunset, so aim for daylight hours. Morning or late afternoon will probably suit the steel best. Part of the sculpture was damaged in a storm in December 2023, so the petals may not be moving when you visit.
card.selfie_here: Try the raised edge of the reflecting pool, in front of the flower's base. Use the front camera, step low toward the water line and tilt the phone up so the flower and its reflection fit in. Fitting two faces and the whole flower is tricky, so keep it low. The northwest corner of the paved walkway is a quieter spot, with the Law School facade as your backdrop. Check on site how the flower sits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on the paved walkway around the pool, so the photo takes in the skyline and trees, while you stand near the pool.
card.rules_and_safety: The flower stands in an open park with paths around it. Check the official site before you go for its current condition and any works.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the flower and its reflection meet in the water, then get a shot where you can't tell which one is the real flower.
card.good_to_know: Floralis Genérica is made of stainless steel and aluminium and has six petals. Architect Eduardo Catalano gave it to the city, and it dates from 2002. It rises out of a round reflecting pool 44 m across. The flower was designed to open in the morning and close at night.

card.hook: Twelve columns, one calm triangle on top, and a huge open square in front. This cathedral almost poses for you, so you don't have to fight for a clear shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de Mayo and face the twelve-column front of the cathedral. Walk back until the whole facade fits in your screen, with a strip of square at the bottom to show how big it is.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full facade with the square in front. Try 0.5x if you're close or want more of the square, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for just the columns and the pediment.

card.best_time: The facade is usually well lit at night, so an evening visit can look great. By day, pick a moment when the square isn't crowded so the front stays clean in your shot.

card.good_to_know: MALBA opened on 21 September 2001. Eduardo Costantini set it up around his own collection of Latin American art. The design won an open competition with 450 proposals from 45 countries, and the winners were three young Argentinian architects: Gaston Atelman, Martin Fourcade and Alfredo Tapia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, out on the street side of Avenida Figueroa Alcorta, then keep walking back until the whole building fits. Face the museum so the sky sits at the top of your screen and a bit of foreground sits at the bottom.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot with MALBA behind the photographer, or a specific passer-by spot for a photo of the visitor with the whole building. The closest mention is a photo caption on wander-argentina.com (https://wander-argentina.com/malba/) describing the museum at night with a water fountain in front, but it names no spot and gives no camera position, so I did not use it. Vivelaversion's Instagram guide (https://vivelaversion.com/the-22-most-instagrammable-places-in-buenos-aires-the-ultimate-guide/) only suggests the sleek exterior and gallery interiors. The address is Av. Presidente Figueroa Alcorta 3415, Palermo, and the Palermo Chico mansions around MALBA are described on buenosairesfreewalks.com (https://buenosairesfreewalks.com/barrios/palermo/what-to-do-in-palermo/), but no page links them to a photo position. Photography rules I found are about the inside of the museum, not selfie sticks or tripods: LorenziGo (https://lorenzigo.com/malba-buenos-aires-museum-guide/) says no flash and that some temporary exhibitions restrict photography, and Wonderful Museums (https://www.wonderfulmuseums.com/museum/malba-art-museum-buenos-aires/) says non-flash photography is generally allowed in the permanent collection. Neither mentions selfie sticks or tripods, so I left the rules list empty. Searches also returned Palermo in Sicily and Palermo Soho results, which I excluded. A local check at the site would be needed before using any spot.

card.hook: Most gardens give you one pretty thing to photograph. This one crams a red bridge, a waterfall, a torii gate and a pagoda-like tower around one pond, so you barely have to move.
card.stand_here: Walk onto the Puente Plano, the flat red bridge near the Hokkaido entrance. Face back over the pond toward the arched red bridge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the arched bridge, its reflection, the waterfall and the Torre de los 13 Aleros in one frame. If the path is busy, drop to 0.5x to squeeze in more. For details like the tower or the torii gate, try zoom 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and set the arched bridge along a lower line, keeping water in front of you so the reflection shows.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when it's quieter, according to one photo guide. Weekends and sunny days get crowded, and people sometimes stand on the path in front of the waterfall, so wait for a gap and take a few frames.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the arched red bridge over the koi pond, slightly off-centre, so the bridge curve, water and greenery all fit behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you want more in, and keep the pond at your back.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't step on the grass, climb the waterfall or rocks, or enter restricted areas. There's not much shade, so bring sunscreen and a hat on sunny days.
card.challenge: Walk slowly and look back across the water from each bridge, then see if you can get three photos that look like three different gardens.
card.good_to_know: The garden is built around a pond, with red bridges, a small waterfall, a vermilion torii gate on a tiny island and the tall Torre de los 13 Aleros. The Puente Plano is the first bridge most visitors cross, according to guides. There's an admission fee, so check the official site for current opening times and tickets.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk onto the Puente Plano, the flat red bridge near the Hokkaido entrance. Face back over the pond toward the arched red bridge.

card.hook: Picture a slice of London standing above the plane trees of Buenos Aires: a tall, narrow tower of pale stone with a clock face. Most people only notice it when it pops out over the treetops, so step back and let the whole thing fit.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza San Martín, across the plaza from the tower, and face it. You'll see it rise above the trees with the Sheraton hotel alongside.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower, the trees and the Sheraton in one shot. Try 1x for a calmer, more natural look, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the clock face and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the tower upright, tap the tower, then slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out the pale stone.
card.best_time: Afternoon is likely to suit this view best, because the sun is behind you and lights up the tower's face. Going when the plaza is quieter helps too.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps beside the Falklands memorial on the Plaza San Martín side, then climb to the top of the hill. One reviewer calls it the best view of the tower area, with a wide vista over the trees. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and check on site which way the tower sits behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot you from the terrace above the Malvinas memorial, where the clock tower is in view across the road in Plaza Fuerza Aérea Argentina.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your bag closed while you take photos, as pickpocketing is a known problem near Retiro station and the bus terminal. Plaza Fuerza Aérea Argentina is reported to be dangerous at night, so visit by day. Access inside the tower varies, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly upright on the gridlines with a tree on each side, then take a second shot of just the clock face. Bonus points if the sky stays blue!
card.good_to_know: Buenos Aires's British community gave the tower to the city to mark the centenary of the May Revolution, and it opened on 24 May 1916. Some people still call it Torre de los Ingleses. Its white Portland stone was shipped from England, and its clock and bells imitate those at Westminster Abbey.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza San Martín, across the plaza from the tower, and face it. You'll see it rise above the trees with the Sheraton hotel alongside.

card.hook: Here's a building that was trimmed, rebuilt and still looks calm about it. The Cabildo's white arches are so simple that even a quick snap looks good.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de Mayo, on the south side of the square near the Cabildo. The Cabildo is about 160 m to the west, so face west and shoot across the open space.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the square so the whole front and tower fit. If the square is busy or you're close, drop to 0.5x and keep your phone level. Then try 2x to pick out the arches and tower.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: A guide to the square suggests late afternoon, but that tip is really about the Casa Rosada. The Cabildo may not be as brightly lit as the pink building next door.
card.selfie_here: Try Avenida de Mayo, about 15 m from the Cabildo. Use the front camera, stand diagonally to the building and keep it at one edge of the frame. The city's own photo guide says afternoon light is best here.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the open square facing the Cabildo and shoot it head-on, with you in front of the facade (no exact spot on the square is marked, so just stand back far enough to fit the whole front).
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, flash may be restricted near documents and paintings, so check the signs. Pickpockets can work crowded spots, especially when tour groups gather near the Cabildo and the Casa Rosada fence, so keep your bag in front of you.
card.challenge: Take three frames with the tower sitting dead straight on a grid line, then pick the one with the fewest strangers walking through.
card.good_to_know: The Cabildo was handed over for use in 1748, and the tower came in 1773, though some accounts say 1764. Three arches were demolished when Avenida de Mayo opened in 1889 and three more in 1931, so only five of the originals remain. The colonial look, including the tower and red roof tiles, was rebuilt in 1939-40 from old documents, and it reopened in October 1940.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de Mayo, on the south side of the square near the Cabildo. The Cabildo is about 160 m to the west, so face west and shoot across the open space.

card.hook: You'd swear this is a French palace that got lost on its way to Paris, but it's actually a waterworks, and it's covered in more than 300,000 glazed, multi-coloured tiles. It fills a whole city block, so getting it all in one photo is the fun part.
card.stand_here: Go to the northeast corner of the block, where Calle Riobamba meets Avenida Córdoba. Face the corner of the palace so both facades run away from you in one diagonal view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because the building is too big for 1x from the street. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched shot of one section, then use 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for the tiles, shields and roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the palace corner on one grid line, and keep the building's vertical lines parallel to the screen edge so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon usually makes the glazed tiles glow. Any bright, clear daytime works, but try to skip the harshest midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Avenida Córdoba pavement between Riobamba and Ayacucho, with the tiled facade right behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little high so the palace fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the public pavement. For the museum or any photos inside, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole corner, then hunt down a close-up of one of the 14 provincial shields up on the roof line.
card.good_to_know: The palace was inaugurated in 1894 to hold the city's water tanks, and it still works as a pumping station. The tiles were made by Royal Doulton in Britain, and the shields up top represent the 14 Argentine provinces of the time. It was declared a National Historic Monument in 1989.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the northeast corner of the block, where Calle Riobamba meets Avenida Córdoba. Face the corner of the palace so both facades run away from you in one diagonal view.

selfie_spots.why: The exterior facade is described as the main photo opportunity, and this Córdoba stretch is the frontage the palace is known by.

card.hook: A big green dome, a fountain crowded with angels and animals, and a whole open square to back up into. This is one of the easier "get the whole building in" spots in Buenos Aires.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza del Congreso, around the central fountain area in front of the building. Face the palace so the Monumento a los Dos Congresos and its sculptures sit in front of you and the green dome rises behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the facade, dome and sculptures in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome and sculpture details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome on the centre line with the sculptures along the bottom third, and keep your phone level so the columns don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday. The building is also lit at night, so it's worth a second visit. Use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the plaza next to the Monumento a los Dos Congresos fountain, with the palace behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low so the dome fits over your shoulder. The bronze of The Thinker, also in the plaza, makes a fun alternative with the Congress behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the median (the central strip) of Avenida de Mayo at the Congress end, shooting toward the palace, while you stand in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is a frequent protest site and building work can limit access, so check the situation when you arrive. If you go inside on a tour, photos are generally fine without flash, but filming is prohibited and guides may restrict photos in some rooms.
card.challenge: Get the dome and the sculptures in one frame with nobody wandering through the foreground, then sneak in a close-up of the Kilometre Zero milestone as your bonus shot.
card.good_to_know: The Argentine National Congress is home to a 72-seat Senate and a 257-seat Chamber of Deputies. It stands at the western end of Avenida de Mayo, with the Casa Rosada at the far end of the same avenue. A milestone marking Kilometre Zero for Argentina's national highways sits in the plaza next to the building.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza del Congreso, around the central fountain area in front of the building. Face the palace so the Monumento a los Dos Congresos and its sculptures sit in front of you and the green dome rises behind them.
